questions.subject: MARKETING
questions.stem: Verdant Beverages, a family-owned firm sells 7 distinct product lines in Westhaven, and each line carries 6 different items. What is the total number of items in the product mix?
questions.explanation: The total number of items, the depth of the whole mix, is the number of product lines multiplied by the number of items in each line: 7 times 6 equals 42. Adding the two figures would mix a count of lines with a count of per-line items, and quoting either number alone captures only part of the mix.
questions.hint: Each line holds several items, so multiply.

options.misconception: counts only the product lines
counts only the items in one line

questions.subject: MARKETING
questions.stem: In Marovia, a blind test finds that most buyers cannot tell Lakeshore Apparel, a fast-growing firm's product from a generic version, yet they pay more for the branded one when they see the label. What does this reveal about the brand?
questions.explanation: Brand equity is the commercial value that comes from the name and associations, not just the physical product. If buyers pay more for the labelled version despite the products being indistinguishable in a blind test, the brand itself is adding value through trust, familiarity or image. That extra willingness to pay is the essence of brand equity.
questions.hint: Ask why buyers pay more when the physical product is the same.
questions.learningObjective: recognise brand equity and its sources

options.text: The brand has no value because the products are identical
options.misconception: ignores the extra willingness to pay created by the label

options.text: Price is the only thing that matters to buyers
options.misconception: overlooks the role of brand associations

options.text: The generic product is of higher quality
options.misconception: confuses an inability to taste a difference with quality

options.text: The brand has equity because of associations and perceived value beyond the physical product

questions.subject: MARKETING
questions.stem: Sales of Pemberton Packaging, a privately held firm's product in Nettleford are rising rapidly, profits are still negative because of heavy launch spending, and only early adopters have bought. Which life-cycle stage is this?
questions.explanation: The introduction stage is marked by low sales, heavy promotional and development costs, and negative profits, with mainly innovators and early adopters buying. The rapid sales growth here might tempt a growth label, but growth normally follows once the product is accepted and profits begin to turn positive. Decline would show falling sales, not a new launch.
questions.hint: Heavy launch costs and only early adopters point to the earliest stage.

options.misconception: confuses early losses with falling sales
mistakes rapid sales growth with early-adopter only distribution for the growth stage
assumes slow growth and established profits
